Tonality is the organizational system underlying most Western music from roughly 1650 to 1900, in which all melodic and harmonic material gravitates toward a single pitch center called the tonic or home key. Built on the major and minor scales, tonality creates a hierarchy of musical relationships: tension and resolution, harmonic movement and return. It is the language of Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, and most music heard in concert halls today.

Tonality centers all musical motion on a single pitch, the tonic. The major and minor scales define the pitches that belong to a key, and chords are built from these scale degrees. The major scale follows a whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half pattern and sounds bright and resolved. The minor scale is darker and more ambiguous, with three variants—natural, harmonic, and melodic—used for different expressive effects. A key signature, the sharps or flats at the start of a staff, signals which tonal center and scale the music inhabits. A key signature of no sharps or flats indicates either C major or A minor.

Harmonic function explains the roles chords play in tonal music. The tonic chord, marked as I, is home. The subdominant, marked as IV, moves away from home. The dominant, marked as V, creates tension, pulling back to I. This tension-release cycle is the engine of tonal music. Modulation is the shift from one key to another within a piece—a temporary visit to a new tonal center—and it provides both structure and surprise.

Tonality emerged during the Baroque era, from 1600 to 1750, as composers adopted the equal temperament tuning system, which made it practical to play in all keys on keyboard instruments. Atonality and the twelve-tone technique, pioneered by Arnold Schoenberg in the early twentieth century, rejected tonality's hierarchy, treating all twelve chromatic pitches as equal. This marked the end of the common-practice era and opened the door to twentieth-century musical modernism.
